summary: Legal limits on what a lawyer may charge, by program and jurisdiction: workers' compensation in every US state and DC, Social Security (SSDI and SSI), the Federal Tort Claims Act, VA benefits, Longshore, FECA and black lung, plus medical-malpractice and general contingency-fee rules in the states read so far. Each record gives the cap type, percent, dollar cap or sliding-scale tiers, what the percent applies to and who approves the fee, and cites the statute, rule or agency page with an exact quote and the date read (P, D or U; no secondary sources). A lookup, not a fee calculator.

sources.label: SSA notice, 89 FR 40523 (2024-05-10)
sources.quote: We are increasing the maximum dollar amount limit for fee agreements approved under the Social Security Act (the Act) to $9,200.

sources.label: SSA notice, 90 FR 19241 (2025-05-06)
sources.quote: With the publication of this Notice the $9,200 fee cap will remain in effect

sources.label: 42 U.S.C. 406(a)(2)(A) (US Code 2024, GPO)
sources.quote: the fee specified in the agreement does not exceed the lesser of

sources.label: 42 U.S.C. 406(a)(2)(A)(ii)(I)
sources.quote: 25 percent of the total amount of such past-due benefits (as determined before any applicable reduction

records.note: The statute's own figure is $4,000; the Commissioner raises it by Federal Register notice. A Federal Register API search on 2026-10-25 found no notice after 90 FR 19241, which says SSA will publish only when it raises the cap. SSA's own fee-agreement page (ssa.gov) returned 403 to our script and was not used. Fees outside the agreement process go through a fee petition.

records.text: For work in federal court on a Social Security case, the statute lets the court allow a reasonable fee of no more than 25% of past-due benefits, separate from any agency-level fee.

sources.label: 42 U.S.C. 406(b)(1)(A) (US Code 2024, GPO)
sources.quote: a reasonable fee for such representation, not in excess of 25 percent of the total of the past-due benefits

sources.label: Culbertson v. Berryhill (2019), syllabus (supremecourt.gov)
sources.quote: Thus, the 25% cap applies only to fees for representation before the court, not the agency.

sources.label: Arizona Revised Statutes § 23-1069 (Arizona Legislature)
sources.quote: shall be not more than twenty-five per cent up to ten years from the date of the award.

records.text: The statute says fees need the Workers' Compensation Commission's approval and are 25% of indemnity benefits; when the claim was contested, the employer or carrier pays half and the worker half.

sources.label: Ark. Code Ann. § 11-9-715(a)(1)(B), as quoted by the Full Commission (AWCC No. H004171, April 11, 2024)
sources.quote: Attorney’s fees shall be twenty-five percent (25%) of compensation for indemnity benefits payable to the injured employee or dependents of a deceased employee

sources.label: Ark. Code Ann. § 11-9-715(a)(1)(A), as quoted by the Full Commission (AWCC No. H004171)

records.text: Colorado's statute says a contingent fee above 25% of the contested benefits is presumed unreasonable in a contested case that is not appealed.

sources.label: C.R.S. § 8-43-403 (Colorado Revised Statutes 2024, Office of Legislative Legal Services PDF)
sources.quote: On unappealed contested cases, a contingent fee exceeding twenty-five percent of the amount of contested benefits is presumed to be unreasonable.

sources.label: C.R.S. § 8-43-403(2)
sources.quote: Any attorney who represents any party in a workers' compensation case shall provide the party with a written fee agreement

records.note: 25% is a presumption, not an absolute bar: the director may approve more if the case was appealed or took an extraordinary amount of time. No contingent fee on previously incurred medical benefits in a permanent disability award. Text is from the 2024 CRS printout (labelled uncertified); the 2025 edition was not found at the same path. Secondary sources often say 20%; the statute we read says 25%.
records.base: the amount of contested benefits (unappealed contested cases)
formalities: written fee agreement

records.text: Delaware's statute says the board awards a reasonable fee of up to 30% of the award or 10 times the state's average weekly wage, whichever is smaller.

sources.label: 19 Del. C. § 2320(10) (Delaware Code Online)
sources.quote: A reasonable attorneys' fee in an amount not to exceed 30 percent of the award or 10 times the average weekly wage in Delaware

records.text: Florida's statute says a judge must approve any fee, and the fee equals 20% of the first $5,000 of benefits, 15% of the next $5,000 and 10% after that (5% after 10 years).

sources.label: Fla. Stat. § 440.34 (2026, The Florida Senate)
sources.quote: must equal to 20 percent of the first $5,000 of the amount of the benefits secured, 15 percent of the next $5,000

sources.label: Fla. Stat. § 440.34(7)
sources.quote: the judge of compensation claims may approve an alternative attorney’s fee not to exceed $1,500 only once per accident

records.note: Approval is by the judge of compensation claims. For disputed medical-only claims a judge may approve an alternative fee up to $1,500 at $150 an hour. The Florida Supreme Court has held the mandatory schedule unconstitutional as applied where it yields an unreasonable fee (Castellanos v. Next Door Co., 2016); that ruling was not re-read here, so treat the schedule as the statute's text, not the whole law.

records.text: Georgia's board rules say a lawyer's fee contract filed with the board may not be more than 25% of the weekly benefits recovered.
